title: The history of understanding the stomach
tagline: Two thousand years from a digestive fire and a cooking pot to a hole in a fur trader’s side, a doctor who drank a germ, and the hunger hormone.
intro: For most of history people pictured the stomach as a warm pot that cooks food. In the 1700s experimenters fed birds metal tubes and swallowed bags of food to test whether it grinds or dissolves. A musket accident gave one doctor a window into a living stomach, chemists found its acid and its enzyme, and physiologists found the nerves and hormones that control it. In the 20th century flexible scopes let doctors look inside, pills turned down the acid, and two Australians showed that most ulcers are caused by a germ.

eras.name: Fire and cooking
eras.summary: Ayurveda’s digestive fire and Galen’s cooking pot: the stomach is pictured as a place of heat.

eras.name: Grind or dissolve?
eras.summary: Chemists and naturalists test whether the stomach crushes food or dissolves it, with birds, tubes and their own stomachs.

eras.name: A window into the stomach
eras.summary: A wounded fur trader, the discovery of hydrochloric acid and pepsin, and the first looks inside.

eras.name: Nerves and hormones
eras.summary: X-rays show the stomach churning, Pavlov shows nerves switch it on, and gastrin shows it sends itself chemical messages.

eras.name: Looking in, turning acid down
eras.summary: Bendable scopes, cameras and glass fibres let doctors see inside, including in India, and new medicines reduce acid.

eras.name: A germ and a hunger hormone
eras.summary: H. pylori overturns what doctors believed about ulcers, and the stomach turns out to help control appetite.

events.date: c. 2nd century BCE to 2nd century CE (dates uncertain)
events.title: Agni, the digestive fire
events.text: The Charaka Samhita, a founding text of Ayurveda put together over several centuries, pictures digestion as the work of agni, a fire inside the body. Its main fire, jatharagni, burns in the belly and is said to rule all the others.
events.why: Digestion as heat that transforms food became one of the oldest and longest-lasting ideas about the stomach.

events.title: Galen’s stomach “concocts” food
events.text: Galen taught that the stomach draws food in, holds it and cooks it with the body’s own heat into a juice, a process called concoction, before pushing it on. The juice was thought to go to the liver to be made into blood. His books were followed for well over a thousand years.
events.why: The idea of the stomach as a warm cooking pot shaped medicine until experiments in the 1700s.

events.title: An acid ferment
events.text: The Flemish chemist van Helmont argued that food is not simply cooked. He proposed that an acid “ferment” in the stomach turns it into something new. His writings were published by his son four years after he died.
events.why: It moved the question from heat to chemistry.

events.title: A bird of prey swallows metal tubes
events.text: Réaumur fed a tame bird of prey (usually described as a kite or buzzard) small metal tubes with holes, filled with meat. The tubes protected the meat from being crushed, yet when the bird coughed them up the meat had partly dissolved. He also had it swallow sponges on threads to collect its stomach juice.
events.why: It showed that digestion is more than grinding: a juice dissolves food.

events.title: Spallanzani swallows his own experiments
events.text: The Italian priest and scientist Spallanzani swallowed small linen bags and pierced wooden tubes holding food, and got them back to see what had happened. He collected gastric juice and showed it could digest meat in a glass outside the body, published in 1780.
events.why: Digestion in a glass proved it is a chemical process, not life-force or cooking.

events.title: A candle-lit tube to look inside
events.text: Bozzini built the Lichtleiter, a “light conductor”: a candle, a mirror and a set of tubes for looking into body openings. The medical faculty in Vienna dismissed it as a curiosity.
events.why: It was the first attempt at an endoscope, the tool doctors now use to look inside the stomach.

events.title: A gunshot leaves a window into the stomach
events.who: Alexis St. Martin and William Beaumont
events.text: A musket went off by accident at close range and wounded Alexis St. Martin, a young French-Canadian fur trader. The army surgeon William Beaumont saved his life, but the wound healed with a permanent opening, a fistula, from his stomach to the skin.
events.why: For the first time, a living human stomach could be watched at work.

events.title: The acid is hydrochloric acid
events.text: The English doctor and chemist Prout analysed stomach contents from animals and showed that the acid is hydrochloric acid, the same acid chemists made from sea salt. He presented the paper to the Royal Society in December 1823.
events.why: It named the stomach’s strongest weapon.

events.title: 238 experiments through a hole
events.where: Fort Niagara, Plattsburgh and other posts
events.text: Over eight years Beaumont dangled pieces of food on silk threads into St. Martin’s stomach, pulled them out to see how far they had digested, and drew off gastric juice to digest food in jars. In 1833 he published Experiments and Observations on the Gastric Juice.
events.why: It proved gastric juice digests food chemically and that the stomach churns, and it became a classic of physiology.

events.title: Pepsin gets its name
events.text: Schwann found a substance in gastric juice, different from the acid, that breaks down egg white and meat. He named it pepsin, from the Greek word for digestion. It was one of the first enzymes ever described.
events.why: It showed that the acid has a partner that does much of the protein cutting.

events.title: A sword swallower’s stomach
events.text: Kussmaul pushed a straight, rigid metal tube, lit from outside by a lamp, down the throat of a professional sword swallower and looked into his stomach. It worked, but the light was poor and the tube dangerous for ordinary patients.
events.why: It was the first look inside a living human stomach through the mouth.

events.title: A word for the stomach’s chemists
events.text: Kühne coined the word “enzyme”, from Greek for “in yeast”, for substances like pepsin that speed up chemical changes without being alive themselves.
events.why: Pepsin, amylase and lipase got a family name.

events.title: Watching the stomach churn on X-ray
events.text: Soon after X-rays were discovered, the medical student Walter Cannon fed animals food mixed with bismuth salts, which show up on X-ray, and watched waves of squeezing sweep across their stomachs. His first paper appeared in the first issue of the American Journal of Physiology.
events.why: It revealed peristalsis and the stomach’s mixing, and led to the barium meal X-ray.

events.title: Nobel Prize for the digestive glands
events.text: Pavlov studied dogs with small surgical pouches of stomach and showed that the sight, smell and taste of food start gastric juice flowing, through nerves including the vagus nerve. He won the Nobel Prize “in recognition of his work on the physiology of digestion”, years before his famous work on conditioned reflexes.
events.why: It showed that the brain and nerves switch digestion on.

events.title: A hormone that calls for acid
events.text: Edkins found that extracts of the lower stomach lining make the stomach produce acid, and suggested a hormone, which he called gastrin.
events.why: It showed the stomach sends itself chemical messages as well as nerve signals.

events.title: A gastroscope that bends
events.text: The doctor Rudolf Schindler and the instrument maker Georg Wolf built a semi-flexible gastroscope, with many small lenses in a tube that could bend a little. It made looking into the stomach much safer.
events.why: It turned gastroscopy into an everyday test for the first time.

events.title: A camera inside the stomach
events.text: At a time when stomach cancer was the leading cause of death in Japan, the surgeon Tatsuro Uji asked Olympus for a camera that could photograph the stomach from inside. With the engineer Mutsuo Sugiura they built the gastrocamera, a tiny camera and flash bulb on the tip of a flexible tube.
events.why: Photographs of the stomach lining helped doctors spot cancers early.

events.title: Light through glass fibres
events.text: Working with the physicist Wilbur Peters and the student Larry Curtiss, the South African-born doctor Hirschowitz made a flexible scope from a bundle of thin glass fibres that carry light around bends. He first passed it down his own throat, then a patient’s a few days later. Production models followed in 1960.
events.why: The flexible fibreoptic endoscope changed gastroenterology for good.

events.title: Gastrin is isolated
events.text: Sixty years after Edkins guessed it existed, Hilda Tracy and Roderic Gregory purified gastrin from pig stomachs and worked out what it is made of.
events.why: It proved the stomach’s acid hormone was real.

events.title: Endoscopy comes to India
events.where: AIIMS New Delhi and PGI Chandigarh
events.text: Diagnostic endoscopy was started in the early and mid-1970s at central institutes, the Postgraduate Institute in Chandigarh and the All India Institute of Medical Sciences in New Delhi, with B. N. Tandon at AIIMS among the pioneers. Specialist gastroenterology departments grew in Mumbai, Kolkata and elsewhere.
events.why: It brought the new flexible scopes to one of the world’s largest populations.

events.title: A pill that turns down acid
events.who: James Black and colleagues at Smith, Kline & French
events.text: Cimetidine (Tagamet) blocks the histamine signal that tells parietal cells to make acid. Launched in the UK in 1976, it let many ulcers heal without surgery. James Black shared the 1988 Nobel Prize.
events.why: It began the era of acid-reducing medicines.

events.title: Curved germs where none should live
events.text: The pathologist Robin Warren kept seeing small curved bacteria on stomach biopsies, always with inflammation. Textbooks said nothing could live in stomach acid.
events.why: One careful observer refused to ignore what he saw.

events.title: The germ is grown
events.text: The young doctor Barry Marshall joined Warren and tried to grow the bacteria. The cultures only succeeded when some plates were left over the long Easter weekend: the germ grows slowly. It was later named Helicobacter pylori.
events.why: It gave the germ a name and let others test the claim.

events.title: A doctor drinks the bacteria
events.text: Few believed that a germ causes stomach disease, and there was no animal model, so Marshall drank a culture of H. pylori himself. Within days he fell ill with a badly inflamed stomach, and a biopsy showed the bacteria had moved in.
events.why: His daring experiment helped convince the world that ulcers can be caused by an infection.

events.title: The first proton pump inhibitor
events.text: Omeprazole, sold as Losec, went on sale in Sweden in 1988. It blocks the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase, the proton pump that parietal cells use to make acid. It became one of the best-selling medicines ever.
events.why: Doctors gained a powerful way to reduce acid for reflux and ulcers.

events.title: Treat the germ, cure the ulcer
events.who: US National Institutes of Health consensus panel
events.text: A US National Institutes of Health panel recommended that ulcer patients infected with H. pylori be treated with antibiotics. The same year the WHO’s cancer agency classified the germ as a cause of stomach cancer.
events.why: Ulcers went from a lifelong illness to one that antibiotics can usually cure.

events.title: The hunger hormone
events.who: Masayasu Kojima, Kenji Kangawa and colleagues
events.text: Kojima and his team discovered ghrelin, a hormone made mainly in the stomach. Later studies showed its level rises before meals and falls after eating, so it became known as the hunger hormone.
events.why: It showed the stomach helps tell the brain when to eat.

events.title: Nobel Prize for H. pylori
events.text: Marshall and Warren won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine “for their discovery of the bacterium Helicobacter pylori and its role in gastritis and peptic ulcer disease”.
events.why: It honoured an idea that most experts had laughed at twenty years earlier.

events.title: Fewer people carry H. pylori
events.who: Yi-Chu Chen, Jyh-Ming Liou and colleagues
events.text: A review of 1,748 studies from 111 countries found that the share of people with H. pylori fell from about 58% in 1980–1990 to about 43% in 2011–2022, though it is still common, especially in children in many countries.
events.why: Stomach ulcers and stomach cancer are becoming rarer in many places as the germ declines.

series.title: Share of people worldwide carrying H. pylori
series.caption: A 2024 review of 1,748 studies from 111 countries: H. pylori infection fell from about 58% of people in 1980–1990 to about 43% in 2011–2022.

facts: Alexis St. Martin, the man with a hole in his stomach, lived to 78 and outlived his doctor William Beaumont by 27 years.
Kussmaul’s first look into a living stomach, in 1868, needed a professional sword swallower, who could take a straight metal tube.
Pepsin takes its name from the Greek word for digestion, and was one of the first enzymes ever described.
Barry Marshall drank a culture of H. pylori in 1984 and fell ill within days, which helped win him a Nobel Prize in 2005.
The cells on the surface of the stomach lining are replaced every few days, one reason the stomach doesn’t digest itself.
